managed_contracts.asset: Exact-project container lifecycle authority, fixed service/client inventory, and separation of browser, Manager, controller, and Docker-engine reachability.
managed_contracts.adversary: A forged, replayed, cross-origin, stale, cross-project, or arbitrary-specification request attempting to control an unapproved container or reach the Docker engine through a UI.
managed_contracts.assumptions: The same-host operator trusts the dedicated root-equivalent controller and Docker engine; loopback browser access is single-operator research access, not production multi-user authentication.
managed_contracts.boundary: The browser reaches the Manager only through host loopback and manager-edge. Manager-to-controller requests use management only; Client self-lifecycle requests use client-lifecycle only. Managed Clients are absent from management and manager-edge, cannot reach the Manager UI/API, and the controller alone mounts the Docker socket. The distinct browser-edge network carries each Client's host-published loopback path and is not a Manager-to-Client network.
managed_contracts.positive_control: One CSRF/origin-valid Manager action on an exact allowlisted project container and one proof-bound Client self-destruction succeed; wrong-project, wrong-instance, replayed, arbitrary-image/command/mount/network/label, and forbidden cross-network controls fail without changing an allowed container.
managed_contracts.expected_observation: Only typed allowlisted actions affect the exact project target, controller status is sanitized, the two lifecycle networks remain disjoint, the two browser-edge networks remain role-specific, and neither UI can contact the Docker socket.
managed_contracts.interpretation_limit: The controller remains root-equivalent same-host operator infrastructure. Network and request checks do not establish independent administration, hostile-local-user isolation, production orchestration security, or availability under Docker-engine compromise.

managed_contracts.asset: Encrypted protected-key backup and authenticated public recovery metadata transported in LOCUS-client-recovery-package-v1 without plaintext key, cue, recovery secret, credential, or party state.
managed_contracts.adversary: A malicious package producer or importer supplying oversized, noncanonical, duplicate, unknown, truncated, digest-mismatched, signature-invalid, stale, cross-subject, cross-epoch, or configuration-override bytes, or inducing export of prohibited secret fields.
managed_contracts.assumptions: The installed trust root, operator signatures, authenticated discovery/current pointer, required current-party quorum, strict codec bounds, and existing storage/admission paths remain available and correct.
managed_contracts.boundary: Export admits only the registered bounded envelope over existing authenticated bytes. Import treats every byte and displayed metadata summary as untrusted until canonical decoding, exact length/digest/signature, subject/epoch, discovery/current-pointer, and current-party checks succeed; package metadata cannot override suite, policy, membership, threshold, endpoint, provider, or fallback behavior.
managed_contracts.positive_control: One canonical package round-trips and reaches descriptor-bound recovery; every single malformed/tampered/stale/substituted mutation fails in its bounded category, and a deliberately inserted private-key, cue, credential, verifier, or party-state field is rejected or detected by the export scan.
managed_contracts.expected_observation: Only an authenticated current package reaches recovery, export contains ciphertext plus permitted public metadata only, and recovery still traverses admission, local storage gateway/provider, current state, authorization, and online threshold parties.
managed_contracts.interpretation_limit: The downloaded package is intentionally persistent outside the Client container and its later file handling is a user/browser boundary. It is not cloud-provider integration, an authenticity root by itself, rollback resistance, an offline backup-only recovery path, or evidence of secure deletion.

managed_contracts.asset: Isolation of dynamic Client identities and volatile server-side private-key, proof, export/import cache, operation, and session state across process lifecycle actions and device-loss destruction.
managed_contracts.adversary: Accidental reuse of Client A memory, proof identity, key slot, session/package state, lifecycle token, writable volume, or public instance identity by a restarted process or newly created recovery Client B.
managed_contracts.assumptions: Managed Clients use the fixed read-only template and no client-scoped durable secret volume; downloaded packages are held outside the destroyed container and explicitly re-imported.
managed_contracts.boundary: Client stop gracefully ends the process and kill ends it abruptly; both make the endpoint unavailable while retaining the container, loopback port binding, lifecycle token, and public client ID. A later start, and every restart, creates a fresh process proof identity with an empty server-side key slot, export/import cache, and operation/session set under that same client ID. Destroy removes the exact container and public ID; a later create obtains a distinct client ID, lifecycle token, and proof identity with no inherited Client A state.
managed_contracts.positive_control: A deliberate server-side volatile marker and loaded synthetic key disappear after stop/start, restart, and kill/start while the public client ID remains and proof identity changes; destroy removes the endpoint/container, and a fresh Client B has a new ID/proof identity and rejects an inherited-state marker or another client's self-lifecycle token.
managed_contracts.expected_observation: Every process re-entry begins with an empty key slot and fresh proof identity, destruction removes the exact Client instance, and only explicit package import plus authenticated remote state enables Client B recovery.
managed_contracts.interpretation_limit: Stop, restart, and kill are destructive volatile resets, not session continuity. Container destruction is bounded state isolation rather than forensic erasure; browser downloads, screen capture, host memory, Docker-engine access, and remote party/provider state remain outside this disposal claim.

managed_contracts.asset: Synthetic plaintext private key and transient cue-derived secret path intentionally exposed only to the active managed Client/browser when the user generates, reveals, or recovers that key.
managed_contracts.adversary: Accidental propagation of the displayed key through Manager/controller APIs, lifecycle messages, package export, service traffic, logs, telemetry, browser storage/history/cache, crash output, screenshots, or later Client processes.
managed_contracts.assumptions: The demonstration uses only generated synthetic keys; the active browser, operating system, and user-visible screen are inside the trusted active-client boundary for the duration of display.
managed_contracts.boundary: The key may appear in the active Client response and DOM only. It is prohibited from Manager/controller data, recovery-package bytes, remote service payloads beyond the existing encrypted/protocol path, durable Client state, browser persistence, logs, crash output, retained screenshots, and evidence. Stop/start, restart, kill/start, and destroy clear the process-local key slot; a newly loaded Client document begins empty.
managed_contracts.positive_control: A fictional key marker is visible in the active Client UI, then output/state/browser-storage/package/network scans detect any deliberate insertion into each prohibited channel and verify absence from the new server process and a newly loaded document after every volatile reset or destruction transition.
managed_contracts.expected_observation: The active Client can visibly compare the generated and recovered synthetic key identity, while every non-client, new-process, and newly loaded post-reset view remains marker-free and the Manager sees only sanitized public lifecycle metadata.
managed_contracts.interpretation_limit: Intentional on-screen display permits observation by the user, screen capture, accessibility tooling, extensions, a malicious browser/OS, or memory inspection. A document already loaded in the external browser can remain rendered until it is closed or reloaded even after its container stops. This is a demonstrability feature, not endpoint-confidentiality, secure-erasure, or usability evidence.

managed_contracts.asset: Synthetic integrated trust root, role TLS identities, signing/proof material, lifecycle-controller secret, and their binding to one exact managed manifest and project state.
managed_contracts.adversary: Silent reuse of expired, incomplete, cross-manifest, or partially reset credentials; accidental credential rotation that strands persistent protocol state; or an operator treating emergency volume deletion as a normal stop.
managed_contracts.assumptions: The local Docker volume boundary and networkless bootstrap role are trusted, the host clock is correct, and the managed research profile is intentionally short-lived rather than a production PKI.
managed_contracts.boundary: A fresh managed bootstrap creates a 366-day CA and 365-day role TLS certificates. Normal Manager stop and emergency integrated-stop without --reset-state preserve exact-project role volumes and credentials; restart reuses them only when the manifest and role-root inventory validate. No in-place renewal is provided. Expired or incompatible state fails closed and requires explicit integrated-stop --reset-state, which deletes all exact-project role/provider volumes so the next start creates a new trust domain and empty protocol state.
managed_contracts.positive_control: Default stop/start preserves certificate serials and enrolled state; an incompatible manifest or expired-certificate fixture fails closed; explicit --reset-state removes the exact role volumes, changes trust/certificate identities on the next start, and leaves no old provider/party state.
managed_contracts.expected_observation: Credentials are neither silently rotated nor partially mixed. Reset is explicit, exact-project scoped, and visibly destructive; a package from the erased deployment cannot recover without its deleted remote epoch state.
managed_contracts.interpretation_limit: The one-year research lifetime and full-state reset are not automated renewal, high-availability rotation, revocation, production PKI, backup migration, or forensic erasure. Reset intentionally destroys local recoverability for prior packages unless an independently preserved compatible deployment still exists.
